title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 13: Obosa v. Court of Appeals: Authority to Approve Bail Bonds in Appealed Cases
keywords: Court of Appeals special five-person Division
primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Obosa v. Court of Appeals, his unanimous ponencia holding that a trial court loses the power to approve a bail bond and order release once the appeal has been perfected, and that an accused charged with a non-bailable offense but convicted of a bailable one is not entitled to bail as a matter of right.

The rule the case produced: discretion over bail in an appealed capital case in which the conviction was for a lesser, bailable crime belongs to the appellate court, not the court of origin -- a stand later written into Section 5 of Rule 114 during the Court's July-September 2000 revision of the Rules on Criminal Procedure.

CJP's answer to the academic criticism that the trial court keeps jurisdiction until the records are transmitted, weighing that doctrinal and practical rule against the special circumstances of an escapee already implicated in a killing while out of prison.

His retrospective vindication of the ruling by two later events -- the Court of Appeals' 1997 conviction of Obosa for double murder with two terms of reclusion perpetua, and the Supreme Court's affirmance in People v. Obosa on May 31, 2000.
sub_topics: The facts: Jose T. Obosa and three others were charged with the double murder of Secretary of Local Governments Jaime N. Ferrer and his driver Jesus D. Calderon, a capital offense for which Obosa was detained without bail throughout trial.

At the time of the killing Obosa was an escapee from the National Penitentiary, serving a term for robbery, having been escorted out by virtue of a subpoena illegally issued by an MTC judge of Sariaya, Quezon.

The Makati RTC convicted him on May 31, 1990 of homicide rather than murder on two counts, granted his manifestation to appeal and to post bail, approved the bond the next day and ordered his release, which the prison authorities carried out on June 4, 1990.

On the OSG's motion a special five-person Division of the Court of Appeals cancelled the bond, nullified the trial court's order and issued a warrant for his immediate arrest, prompting his petition to the Supreme Court.
First ruling: the trial court had authority to grant bail when it did, but not to approve the bond and issue the release order after the appeal had already been perfected.

Second ruling: he was not entitled to bail, because the Information charged murder, a non-bailable offense; under the pre-Administrative Circular 12-94 rules an appeal opens the whole case for review, as Quemel v. CA held, so conviction for the original charge remains possible, and a prior showing that the evidence of guilt is strong subsists on appeal.

The governing principle: while the grant of bail is initially within the trial court's discretion, that discretion must be exercised 'with caution and only for strong reasons,' and it is best lodged in the appellate court in appealed cases.

The criticism: the academe cited the general rule that jurisdiction does not end with the mere filing of a notice of appeal while the records remain below, with the practical point that the appellate court cannot act on documents it does not have.

CJP's counterweight: an escapee charged with murder and convicted of homicide could commit other crimes if released, and would in all probability jump bail if the appellate court raised his conviction to murder with reclusion perpetua.

He declines to fault trial judge Nemesio Felix, whose post-trial judgment was that the crime was bailable homicide, while noting that the Court of Appeals, on a quick review of the records, judged Obosa unworthy of bail since the homicide conviction was not yet final.

The codification: the Court's deliberations from July to September 2000 upheld his stand, adding to Rule 114 a proviso that when the trial court's decision changes the nature of the offense from non-bailable to bailable, the bail application 'can only be filed with and resolved by the appellate court.'

The vindication: on November 27, 1997 the Court of Appeals found Obosa guilty of double murder and imposed two terms of reclusion perpetua, and on May 31, 2000 the Supreme Court affirmed in toto -- had he been bailed and absconded, the appeal would have been dismissed and the homicide judgment would have become final.

stances.claim: Once an appeal has been perfected, the trial court may no longer approve a bail bond or order the accused released; that discretion belongs to the appellate court.
stances.rhetorical_move: jurisdictional line-drawing, separating the power to grant bail from the power to approve the bond afterwards

stances.claim: An accused charged with a non-bailable offense but convicted of a bailable one has no right to bail on appeal, because the appeal reopens the whole case and the earlier finding that the evidence of guilt is strong still subsists.
stances.rhetorical_move: precedent-based reasoning from Quemel on the scope of criminal appeals

stances.claim: Releasing this particular escapee on bail would have been bad judicial policy, since he had already offended while at large and would probably have jumped bail if convicted of murder on appeal.
stances.rhetorical_move: policy weighing of the special circumstances against the general doctrinal rule the critics cited

stances.claim: Subsequent events vindicated the decision: the Court of Appeals convicted Obosa of double murder and the Supreme Court affirmed, so bail would have let him make a mockery of judicial processes.
stances.rhetorical_move: retrospective proof, citing two later judgments as evidence the ruling was right

notable_anecdotes: CJP recounts how Obosa came to be at the scene at all: an escapee from the National Penitentiary escorted out by virtue of a subpoena illegally issued by an MTC judge of Sariaya, Quezon, who claimed he needed to ask about the whereabouts of the accused.
He notes that his unanimous ponencia nonetheless 'drew some flak, especially from the academe,' and sets out the critics' doctrinal and practical objections before answering them.
He goes out of his way to absolve the trial judge, Nemesio Felix, who could not be completely faulted for granting bail because his own post-trial judgment was that the offense was bailable homicide.

He records that the Court, deliberating on the revised Rules from July to September 2000, adopted his stand and wrote it into Rule 114 -- and that the Court of Appeals later convicted Obosa of double murder, with the Supreme Court affirming in toto on May 31, 2000.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' set out Obosa v. Court of Appeals, the unanimous ponencia Artemio V. Panganiban wrote on who may approve bail in an appealed case. Jose T. Obosa, an escapee from the National Penitentiary who had been let out on a subpoena illegally issued by an MTC judge of Sariaya, was charged with the double murder of Secretary of Local Governments Jaime N. Ferrer and his driver Jesus D. Calderon. The Makati RTC convicted him instead of homicide on two counts, granted his manifestation to appeal and post bail, approved the bond the following day and ordered his release, which the prison authorities carried out. On the Solicitor General's motion a special five-person Division of the Court of Appeals cancelled the bond, nullified the order and ordered his arrest. The Supreme Court agreed: the trial court had power to grant bail when it did but not to approve the bond and release him after the appeal was perfected, and Obosa had no right to bail because the Information charged murder, because an appeal in a criminal case opens the whole case for review as Quemel held, and because the earlier showing that the evidence of guilt was strong survived his conviction for a lesser offense. Although the grant of bail is initially the trial court's discretion, CJP wrote, that discretion must be exercised with caution and only for strong reasons, and is best lodged in the appellate court. He answered the academe's objection that jurisdiction persists while the records remain below by weighing the special circumstances of an escapee who could offend again and would probably jump bail, calling his release bad judicial policy, while declining to fault trial judge Nemesio Felix. The Court's July to September 2000 deliberations wrote his stand into Section 5 of Rule 114, and the later conviction of Obosa for double murder, affirmed in toto on May 31, 2000, confirmed that bail would have let him make a mockery of judicial processes.
